rows.description: A child says a project will be quick and starts the night before. He imagines the ideal path and forgets past delays.

rows.subtype: Approach: repeats the same underestimate again and again [Pitfall]
rows.description: A teenager plans to finish revision for a whole subject in one weekend, and misses each time, yet makes the same weekend plan for the next subject.

rows.subtype: Feeling like a fraud in a top college [Actor]
rows.description: A student admitted to a prestigious institute believes they got in by luck and that everyone will soon find out; success is discounted while comparison with others is harsh.

rows.subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
rows.description: A senior colleague notices a capable newcomer who never speaks in meetings. Inviting their view, sharing that everyone once felt lost and giving specific credit help them find a voice.

rows.subtype: Restless and asking what to do [Actor]
rows.description: A child declares boredom after ten minutes and wants a screen; boredom is uncomfortable but can also be the doorway to imagination when adults give time and simple materials.
A school-age child rolls the eyes at a sibling or teacher, signalling boredom, annoyance or dismissal. It may be a way to avoid a spoken argument, and calmly asking what is wrong opens a better talk.
A child who stumbles while reading makes a silly face and gets the class laughing with them; the joke keeps control of the moment, though constant clowning can hide worry.
A teenager uses sarcasm, memes and inside jokes to bond with peers. Shared humour signals who is in the group, and it can also be used to exclude others.
A child insists the cracked cup was never cracked and that they did not spill anything, as if the fact will vanish if unsaid; fear of being in trouble outweighs the wish to be accurate.

A calm friend says "That is not true, please delete it" to those who spread it, and helps the target speak to a teacher or parent. Public denial by the target often fuels the fire, so support matters more than a big reply.
A child who takes longer with reading calls themselves dumb and stops trying; a single label replaces a specific skill that can be practised.

A teacher sees a bright pupil who cannot sit still and blurts answers. Rather than labelling, they adjust seating, give movement breaks and talk with the family about seeking a professional assessment if it seems needed.
